node.label: Tzvetan Todorov
node.date_label: 1982 La Conquête de l’Amérique · 1984 The Conquest of America — Richard Howard’s English translation · 1991 Face à l’extrême
node.description: Tzvetan Todorov connected literary and semiotic inquiry with historical questions about conquest, moral choice and collective memory. La Conquête de l’Amérique uses the encounter between Europeans and Americans to examine relations with others; his short 1984 essay explicitly chooses Mexico as its historical case. Later works address extreme violence and wartime France. In his own essay on memory, commemoration does not automatically prevent renewed violence: narratives of past victimhood can also legitimate aggression. These selected arguments retain their ethical and interpretive character.
node.representative_figures_and_works: La Conquête de l’Amérique: la question de l’autre (1982); The Conquest of America — Richard Howard’s English translation (1984); Face à l’extrême (1991); Une tragédie française, été 1944: scènes de guerre civile (1994).
node.scope_note: The colonial connection uses only three authored opening paragraphs of the 1984 essay, printed 89. The memory connection uses Todorov’s short UNESCO essay. The full 1984 article and historical monographs remain unread. Howard’s 1984 English translation and the 1982 French original are distinct; the 2018 web posting is posthumous. The exact frozen first-author key P:todorov|tzvetan has 125 dated dissertation appearances; this retains the reviewed provisional screening qualification and does not verify every fragment or imply influence. Complete monographs remain unread except the specified selected passages. Existing identities, collective relationships, roster prose and source qualifications remain intact. incident_edges.relationship: Uses conquest as a historical case for examining attitudes toward other societies
incident_edges.evidence_note: The three authored opening paragraphs of “The Morality of Conquest, ” printed 89, explicitly identify the conquest of Mexico and its texts as the case. This limited methodological connection does not assert the unread book’s full thesis or label Todorov a member of a later school.

incident_edges.relationship: Challenges the assumption that remembering victimhood necessarily prevents violence
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own UNESCO essay distinguishes selective remembrance from ethical use and warns that former victims can become aggressors. This is his bounded intervention on public memory, not a psychological finding or a universal judgment on victims.

incident_edges.relationship: Pagden adopts Todorov’s contrast between Spanish initiative and Mexica efforts to maintain the status quo in his particular interpretation of the first sustained encounter, and acknowledges Todorov’s suggestions for improving his work.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Pagden’s introduction, p. lv and note 43, explicitly identifies Todorov’s point; acknowledgments p. vi credit Todorov alongside Richard Kagan and Ángel Delgado Gómez. This is a scoped use and named feedback, not endorsement of every part of Todorov’s conquest thesis or a general claim about Indigenous passivity. Hernán Cortés is the letters’ author; Pagden is translator, editor and introduction author; J. H. Elliott’s introductory essay is separate. Pages were read in the 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition of a work first published in 1971 and revised in 1986. The witness is not backdated to 1971, and the date of each introductory revision is not independently established. Todorov’s original book and the complete letters remain unread.

records.context: Questions how selective public remembrance may serve either responsibility or renewed aggression.

verification.note: Fresh facsimile reading and visual collation: title/copyright leaves, acknowledgments vi (PDF 11), Pagden Introduction lv (PDF 60), including Todorov note 43. Cortés authors the letters; Pagden’s introduction differs from Elliott’s essay. The 2001 edition states original 1971 and revised 1986; exact timing of every introductory revision is not established. No whole-volume or original Todorov-body reading claimed.
